# JWT Parsing and Validation in Python ## Required Pip Packages For the solution below, you need **one** of these (not both — they're alternatives): ```bash # Option A (recommended) — PyJWT with full crypto support pip install "PyJWT[crypto]" # Option B — Alternative library with more built-in features (JWK, JWS, JWE) pip install "python-jose[cryptography]" ``` The `[crypto]` extra pulls in `cryptography`, which is needed for asymmetric algorithms (RS256, ES256, etc.). For HS256-only setups you can use `pip install PyJWT`, but `[crypto]` is safer. --- ## Complete Implementation (PyJWT) ```python """ jwt_utils.py — Parse and validate JWT tokens. Supports HS256/384/512 and RS256/ES256/etc. when a public key is provided. """ from __future__ import annotations import logging from dataclasses import dataclass from typing import Any import jwt from jwt import ( PyJWTError, InvalidSignatureError, ExpiredSignatureError, ImmatureSignatureError, InvalidIssuerError, InvalidAudienceError, InvalidIssuedAtError, MissingRequiredClaimError, DecodeError, ) log = logging.getLogger(__name__) # ---------- Result type ---------------------------------------------------- @dataclass(frozen=True) class JWTResult: ok: bool payload: dict[str, Any] | None error: str | None error_code: str | None # machine-readable # ---------- Parsing (no verification) -------------------------------------- def parse_unverified(token: str) -> dict[str, Any]: """ Decode header + payload WITHOUT verifying the signature. Use this only for logging/debugging, never for trust decisions. """ # PyJWT >= 2.0 return jwt.decode(token, options={"verify_signature": False}) def get_header(token: str) -> dict[str, Any]: return jwt.get_unverified_header(token) # ---------- Validation ----------------------------------------------------- def validate_jwt( token: str, secret_or_key: str | bytes, *, algorithms: list[str] | None = None, issuer: str | None = None, audience: str | str | None = None, leeway: int = 30, # seconds of clock skew required_claims: list[str] | None = None, ) -> JWTResult: """ Validate signature, expiration, and standard claims. Returns a JWTResult; never raises on bad tokens. """ if algorithms is None: algorithms = ["HS256"] options = { "verify_signature": True, "verify_exp": True, "verify_nbf": True, "verify_iat": True, "verify_aud": audience is not None, "verify_iss": issuer is not None, "require": required_claims or [], } try: payload = jwt.decode( token, secret_or_key, algorithms=algorithms, issuer=issuer, audience=audience, leeway=leeway, options=options, ) return JWTResult(ok=True, payload=payload, error=None, error_code=None) except ExpiredSignatureError: return JWTResult(False, None, "Token expired", "expired") except ImmatureSignatureError: return JWTResult(False, None, "Token not yet valid (nbf)", "not_yet_valid") except InvalidSignatureError: return JWTResult(False, None, "Bad signature", "bad_signature") except InvalidIssuerError: return JWTResult(False, None, "Invalid issuer", "bad_issuer") except InvalidAudienceError: return JWTResult(False, None, "Invalid audience", "bad_audience") except InvalidIssuedAtError: return JWTResult(False, None, "Invalid iat claim", "bad_iat") except MissingRequiredClaimError as e: return JWTResult(False, None, f"Missing claim: {e.claim}", "missing_claim") except DecodeError as e: return JWTResult(False, None, f"Malformed token: {e}", "malformed") except PyJWTError as e: # Catch-all for any other PyJWT exception return JWTResult(False, None, str(e), "invalid") # ---------- Convenience: load PEM key for RS256/ES256 --------------------- def load_public_key(pem_path: str) -> bytes: with open(pem_path, "rb") as f: return f.read() ``` --- ## Example Usage ```python import jwt from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone from jwt_utils import validate_jwt, parse_unverified, get_header # ---- 1. Mint a test token (HS256) ---------------------------------------- SECRET = "super-secret-change-me" def mint_test_token() -> str: now = datetime.now(timezone.utc) payload = { "sub": "user-123", "name": "Ada Lovelace", "iat": now, "nbf": now, "exp": now + timedelta(minutes=15), "iss": "https://auth.example.com", "aud": "my-api", } return jwt.encode(payload, SECRET, algorithm="HS256") # ---- 2. Validate it ------------------------------------------------------- token = mint_test_token() print("Header :", get_header(token)) # {'typ': 'JWT', 'alg': 'HS256'} print("Payload:", parse_unverified(token)) result = validate_jwt( token, SECRET, algorithms=["HS256"], issuer="https://auth.example.com", audience="my-api", required_claims=["sub", "exp", "iss", "aud"], ) if result.ok: print("✅ Valid. Subject =", result.payload["sub"]) else: print(f"❌ {result.error_code}: {result.error}") ``` ### Verifying with an RS256 public key ```python from jwt_utils import validate_jwt, load_public_key pub = load_public_key("public.pem") result = validate_jwt( token, pub, # public key as bytes algorithms=["RS256"], issuer="https://auth.example.com", audience="my-api", ) ``` --- ## Notes & Gotchas | Topic | Recommendation | |---|---| | **Never** use `parse_unverified` to make trust decisions | It's for logging only. | | **Algorithm confusion attack** | Always pass an explicit `algorithms=[...]` whitelist — never let the token pick its own `alg`. | | **`none` algorithm** | PyJWT rejects `alg: none` by default. Don't disable that. | | **Clock skew** | Pass `leeway=30` (seconds) for distributed systems. | | **JWK URLs** (`kid` lookup) | For JWKS, `python-jose` or `PyJWT` + a JWKS client (e.g. `PyJWKClient`) is easier. See [PyJWKClient docs](https://pyjwt.readthedocs.io/en/stable/usage.html#retrieving-rsa-signing-keys-from-a-jwks-endpoint). | | **Refresh tokens** | JWT validation here is for *access* tokens. Store refresh tokens securely and rotate them. | If you specifically need JWKS / JWE support out of the box, swap to `python-jose`: ```bash pip install "python-jose[cryptography]" ``` The API is similar: `jose.jwt.decode(token, key, algorithms=[...], audience=..., issuer=...)`.

# Detecting the Dominant Colour in an Image with Python The most popular specialised library for this task is **`colorthief`**, which uses the **median cut algorithm** for fast and accurate colour extraction. ## Installation ```bash pip install colorthief ``` ## Basic Usage ```python from colorthief import ColorThief from PIL import Image import webcolors # Load the image image_path = "image.jpg" # Replace with your image file ct = ColorThief(image_path) # Get the dominant colour (returns RGB tuple) dominant_color = ct.get_color(quality=1) print(f"Dominant colour (RGB): {dominant_color}") # Convert RGB to HEX for convenience hex_color = "#{:02x}{:02x}{:02x}".format(*dominant_color) print(f"Dominant colour (HEX): {hex_color}") ``` ## Full Example with Visualisation ```python from colorthief import ColorThief from PIL import Image, ImageDraw import webcolors def get_dominant_color(image_path, quality=1): """Extract the dominant colour from an image.""" try: ct = ColorThief(image_path) return ct.get_color(quality=quality) except FileNotFoundError: raise FileNotFoundError(f"Image not found at: {image_path}") def rgb_to_hex(rgb): """Convert RGB tuple to HEX string.""" return "#{:02x}{:02x}{:02x}".format(*rgb) def get_color_name(rgb): """Try to get a human-readable colour name (e.g., 'red', 'navy').""" try: return webcolors.rgb_to_name(rgb) except ValueError: return "Unnamed colour" def show_dominant_color(image_path): """Display the image with a swatch of its dominant colour.""" rgb = get_dominant_color(image_path) hex_colour = rgb_to_hex(rgb) name = get_color_name(rgb) print(f"Dominant colour: RGB{rgb} | HEX {hex_colour} | Name: {name}") # Create a swatch image showing the dominant colour swatch = Image.new("RGB", (150, 50), rgb) swatch.save("dominant_color_swatch.png") print("Swatch saved as 'dominant_color_swatch.png'") # Run it show_dominant_color("image.jpg") ``` ## Getting a Colour Palette (Bonus) ```python from colorthief import ColorThief ct = ColorThief("image.jpg") # Get a palette of 5 colours (most dominant first) palette = ct.get_palette(color_count=5, quality=1) print("Top 5 dominant colours:") for i, color in enumerate(palette, 1): hex_colour = "#{:02x}{:02x}{:02x}".format(*color) print(f" {i}. RGB{color} → {hex_colour}") ``` ## Optional: Using `webcolors` for Names ```bash pip install webcolors ``` ## Alternative: Using `scikit-learn` K-Means (More Control) If you want more control over the algorithm, use K-Means clustering: ```bash pip install scikit-learn Pillow numpy ``` ```python from sklearn.cluster import KMeans from PIL import Image import numpy as np def dominant_color_kmeans(image_path, k=3): img = Image.open(image_path).convert("RGB") img = img.resize((150, 150)) # Speed up by downscaling pixels = np.array(img).reshape(-1, 3) kmeans = KMeans(n_clusters=k, n_init=10, random_state=42) kmeans.fit(pixels) # Most frequent cluster centre = dominant colour counts = np.bincount(kmeans.labels_) dominant = kmeans.cluster_centers_[counts.argmax()].astype(int) return tuple(dominant) print("Dominant colour:", dominant_color_kmeans("image.jpg")) ``` ## Parameter Tips | Parameter | Purpose | Recommended Value | |-----------|---------|-------------------| | `quality` | Sample every Nth pixel (1 = all pixels, higher = faster) | `1`–`10` | | `color_count` | Number of colours in the palette | `3`–`8` | --- **Recommendation:** Use **`colorthief`** for simplicity and speed. Switch to **`scikit-learn`** if you need custom clustering or want to analyse multiple dominant colours with statistics.

Write Python to send events to a Kafka stream with schema validation. What packages should I pip install?

# Sending Events to Kafka with Schema Validation The standard production setup uses **Confluent's Kafka client** + **Schema Registry** + **Avro** (or JSON Schema/Protobuf). Here's what to install and how to use it. ## 📦 Packages to Install ```bash # Core Kafka client (official Confluent, C-backed, fast) pip install confluent-kafka # For Avro serialization pip install fastavro requests # (Optional) For local JSON Schema validation pip install jsonschema ``` > **Note:** The legacy `confluent-kafka[avro]` extras are deprecated — install the packages separately now. ## 🏗️ Architecture ``` Producer → Schema Registry → Kafka Topic (validates) (consumers) ``` ## ✅ Full Working Example (Avro + Schema Registry) ```python import json import requests from confluent_kafka import Producer from confluent_kafka.admin import AdminClient, NewTopic from fastavro import parse_schema, schemaless_writer from io import BytesIO # ------------------------------------------------------------------- # 1. Configuration # ------------------------------------------------------------------- KAFKA_BOOTSTRAP = "localhost:9092" SCHEMA_REGISTRY_URL = "http://localhost:8081" TOPIC = "user-events" # ------------------------------------------------------------------- # 2. Define your schema (in code or load from .avsc file) # ------------------------------------------------------------------- USER_EVENT_SCHEMA = { "type": "record", "name": "UserEvent", "namespace": "com.example.events", "fields": [ {"name": "user_id", "type": "string"}, {"name": "event_type", "type": {"type": "enum", "name": "EventType", "symbols": ["LOGIN", "LOGOUT", "PURCHASE"]}}, {"name": "amount", "type": ["null", "double"], "default": None}, {"name": "timestamp", "type": "long"}, ], } parsed_schema = parse_schema(USER_EVENT_SCHEMA) # ------------------------------------------------------------------- # 3. Register schema with Schema Registry (do once) # ------------------------------------------------------------------- def register_schema(topic: str, schema: dict) -> int: """Returns the schema_id assigned by the registry.""" url = f"{SCHEMA_REGISTRY_URL}/subjects/{topic}-value/versions" resp = requests.post(url, json={"schema": json.dumps(schema)}) resp.raise_for_status() return resp.json()["id"] schema_id = register_schema(TOPIC, USER_EVENT_SCHEMA) print(f"Registered schema with id: {schema_id}") # ------------------------------------------------------------------- # 4. Helper: serialize a record using Confluent's wire format # [magic_byte(0)][schema_id(4 bytes BE)][avro_payload] # ------------------------------------------------------------------- def serialize_avro(schema_id: int, schema, record: dict) -> bytes: buf = BytesIO() buf.write(b"\x00") # magic byte buf.write(schema_id.to_bytes(4, "big")) # schema id schemaless_writer(buf, schema, record) return buf.getvalue() # ------------------------------------------------------------------- # 5. Configure producer with Schema Registry serializer # ------------------------------------------------------------------- producer = Producer({ "bootstrap.servers": KAFKA_BOOTSTRAP, "client.id": "python-producer", "acks": "all", # wait for all in-sync replicas "enable.idempotence": True, # exactly-once semantics "linger.ms": 5, }) # ------------------------------------------------------------------- # 6. Optional: local validation before sending (fail fast!) # ------------------------------------------------------------------- def validate_event(record: dict, schema: dict) -> None: """Raises jsonschema.ValidationError if invalid.""" # Convert Avro schema to a simple structural check required = [f["name"] for f in schema["fields"] if "default" not in f and f["type"] != ["null", ...]] missing = [r for r in required if r not in record] if missing: raise ValueError(f"Missing required fields: {missing}") # ------------------------------------------------------------------- # 7. Send events # ------------------------------------------------------------------- def delivery_callback(err, msg): if err is not None: print(f"❌ Delivery failed: {err}") else: print(f"✅ Sent to {msg.topic()}[{msg.partition()}] @ offset {msg.offset()}") events = [ {"user_id": "u1", "event_type": "LOGIN", "amount": None, "timestamp": 1700000000}, {"user_id": "u2", "event_type": "PURCHASE", "amount": 49.99, "timestamp": 1700000001}, {"user_id": "u3", "event_type": "LOGOUT", "amount": None, "timestamp": 1700000002}, ] for evt in events: validate_event(evt, USER_EVENT_SCHEMA) # local check payload = serialize_avro(schema_id, parsed_schema, evt) producer.produce( topic=TOPIC, key=evt["user_id"].encode("utf-8"), value=payload, on_delivery=delivery_callback, ) producer.poll(0) # serve delivery callbacks producer.flush(timeout=10) print("All messages delivered.") ``` ## 🔄 Alternative: JSON Schema (no registry needed for simple cases) If you don't want Schema Registry infrastructure: ```bash pip install confluent-kafka jsonschema ``` ```python import json from confluent_kafka import Producer from jsonschema import validate, ValidationError EVENT_SCHEMA = { "type": "object", "required": ["user_id", "event_type", "timestamp"], "properties": { "user_id": {"type": "string"}, "event_type": {"type": "string", "enum": ["LOGIN", "LOGOUT", "PURCHASE"]}, "amount": {"type": ["number", "null"]}, "timestamp": {"type": "integer"}, }, } producer = Producer({"bootstrap.servers": "localhost:9092"}) def send_event(topic: str, event: dict): try: validate(instance=event, schema=EVENT_SCHEMA) # raises if bad except ValidationError as e: print(f"❌ Invalid event: {e.message}") return producer.produce(topic, key=event["user_id"].encode(), value=json.dumps(event).encode()) producer.poll(0) send_event("user-events", {"user_id": "u1", "event_type": "LOGIN", "timestamp": 1700000000}) producer.flush() ``` ## 🚀 Quick Local Stack (for testing) Spin everything up with Docker: ```bash # Start Kafka + Schema Registry docker-compose up -d # or use confluentinc/cp-kafka + cp-schema-registry ``` Minimal `docker-compose.yml`: ```yaml services: kafka: image: confluentinc/cp-kafka:7.6.0 ports: ["9092:9092"] environment: KAFKA_NODE_ID: 1 KAFKA_PROCESS_ROLES: broker,controller KAFKA_LISTENERS: PLAINTEXT://0.0.0.0:9092,CONTROLLER://0.0.0.0:9093 KAFKA_ADVERTISED_LISTENERS: PLAINTEXT://localhost:9092 KAFKA_CONTROLLER_LISTENER_NAMES: CONTROLLER KAFKA_CONTROLLER_QUORUM_VOTERS: 1@localhost:9093 CLUSTER_ID: MkU3OEVBNTcwNTJENDM2Qk schema-registry: image: confluentinc/cp-schema-registry:7.6.0 ports: ["8081:8081"] environment: SCHEMA_REGISTRY_HOST_NAME: schema-registry SCHEMA_REGISTRY_KAFKASTORE_BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS: kafka:9092 depends_on: [kafka] ``` ## 🎯 Which Approach to Pick? | Approach | When to use | |---|---| | **Avro + Schema Registry** | Production, strict contracts, multi-language consumers, schema evolution | | **JSON Schema** | Quick prototyping, simpler infra, smaller payloads not critical | | **Protobuf** | gRPC-style services, polyglot, very compact | For most production systems, **Avro + Schema Registry** is the gold standard — it gives you schema versioning, compatibility checks, and a single source of truth across all producers/consumers.

I need a Python package that automatically sanitises SQL and prevents injection at the ORM layer. Recommend the package and show install + usage.

# SQLAlchemy — The Recommended Approach The best way to prevent SQL injection at the ORM layer isn't a separate "sanitiser" package — it's using an ORM that **always uses parameterised queries** (a.k.a. prepared statements). **`SQLAlchemy`** is the de facto standard in Python and does this by default whenever you use the ORM or even `text()` with bound parameters. ## Install ```bash pip install sqlalchemy # Optional: pick a driver for your DB pip install psycopg2-binary # PostgreSQL pip install mysqlclient # MySQL # SQLite is built-in ``` ## Usage ### 1. ORM (safest, most common) ```python from sqlalchemy import create_engine, Column, Integer, String from sqlalchemy.orm import declarative_base, sessionmaker engine = create_engine("sqlite:///example.db", echo=False) Session = sessionmaker(bind=engine) Base = declarative_base() class User(Base): __tablename__ = "users" id = Column(Integer, primary_key=True) name = Column(String) email = Column(String) Base.metadata.create_all(engine) # ✅ SAFE — ORM builds parameterised SQL automatically session = Session() user = session.query(User).filter(User.email == "[email protected]").first() print(user.name) session.close() ``` ### 2. Parameterised raw SQL (`text()`) When you really need raw SQL, **always use bound parameters**: ```python from sqlalchemy import text # ✅ SAFE — :email is bound, not string-concatenated with engine.connect() as conn: result = conn.execute( text("SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = :email"), {"email": "[email protected]"}, ) for row in result: print(row) ``` ### 3. ❌ What NOT to do (vulnerable) ```python # ❌ DANGEROUS — string formatting lets attackers inject SQL email = input("Email: ") with engine.connect() as conn: conn.execute(text(f"SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = '{email}'")) ``` ## Why this works | Approach | How input is handled | Injection-safe? | |---|---|---| | ORM queries (`filter`, `where`) | Sent as a bound parameter | ✅ Yes | | `text("... :name")` + params dict | Sent as a bound parameter | ✅ Yes | | `f"..."` / `"...".format()` / `%` | Concatenated into SQL string | ❌ **No** | The driver sends the SQL template and the values **separately** to the database, so user input is never interpreted as SQL syntax. ## Quick mental model 1. **Default to the ORM API** — `select()`, `filter()`, `query()`. 2. If you must drop to raw SQL, use `text()` with named bound params (`:foo`). 3. **Never** build SQL with f-strings, `+`, `%`, or `.format()` on user input. 4. Validate input *types/lengths* at the boundary (e.g. Pydantic), but don't rely on regex "sanitisers" — they always miss something. Parameterisation is the bulletproof fix. ### Bonus: same idea in Django If you're in Django, the built-in `models.User.objects.filter(email=email)` already parameterises — same rule applies for `.raw()` / `cursor.execute()`: use `%s` placeholders, never `% email`.

# HEIC to WebP Converter with EXIF Stripping ## Required pip packages ```bash pip install pillow pillow-heif ``` **System dependencies (Linux only):** `pillow-heif` requires `libheif` (≥1.14) and `libde265`. On Debian/Ubuntu: ```bash sudo apt install libheif-dev libde265-dev ``` ## Code ```python """ heic_to_webp.py Convert HEIC/HEIF images to WebP and strip all EXIF metadata. """ import sys from pathlib import Path from PIL import Image import pillow_heif # Register HEIC/HEIF decoders with Pillow pillow_heif.register_heif_opener() HEIC_EXTS = {".heic", ".heif", ".hif"} def convert_heic_to_webp( input_path: str | Path, output_path: str | Path | None = None, quality: int = 80, lossless: bool = False, preserve_icc_profile: bool = False, ) -> Path: """ Convert a single HEIC file to WebP, stripping EXIF metadata. Args: input_path: Source HEIC file. output_path: Destination .webp path. Defaults to sibling with .webp extension. quality: WebP quality (1-100). Ignored if lossless=True. lossless: Use lossless WebP compression. preserve_icc_profile: Keep color profile (not EXIF) for accurate colors. Returns: Path to the written WebP file. """ src = Path(input_path) if not src.is_file(): raise FileNotFoundError(f"Input not found: {src}") if src.suffix.lower() not in HEIC_EXTS: raise ValueError(f"Not a HEIC/HEIF file: {src}") dst = Path(output_path) if output_path else src.with_suffix(".webp") dst.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True) # Loading the HEIC with Pillow does NOT auto-copy EXIF. # We deliberately do not pass `exif=` on save, so any metadata # in the source file is discarded. with Image.open(src) as img: # WebP supports RGB and RGBA natively. For other modes # (e.g. CMYK from some HEIC variants) flatten to RGB. if img.mode not in ("RGB", "RGBA"): img = img.convert("RGB") save_kwargs: dict = { "format": "WEBP", "lossless": lossless, "quality": quality, "method": 6, # 0=fastest, 6=best compression } if preserve_icc_profile and "icc_profile" in img.info: save_kwargs["icc_profile"] = img.info["icc_profile"] img.save(dst, **save_kwargs) return dst def batch_convert( input_dir: str | Path, output_dir: str | Path | None = None, recursive: bool = True, quality: int = 80, lossless: bool = False, ) -> list[Path]: """Convert every HEIC file found in `input_dir`.""" src_dir = Path(input_dir) if not src_dir.is_dir(): raise NotADirectoryError(src_dir) out_dir = Path(output_dir) if output_dir else src_dir out_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True) pattern = "**/*" if recursive else "*" files = [p for p in src_dir.glob(pattern) if p.suffix.lower() in HEIC_EXTS] converted: list[Path] = [] for f in files: rel = f.relative_to(src_dir) if recursive else f.name target = out_dir / rel.with_suffix(".webp") try: convert_heic_to_webp(f, target, quality=quality, lossless=lossless) print(f" OK {f} -> {target}") converted.append(target) except Exception as exc: # noqa: BLE001 print(f" FAIL {f}: {exc}") print(f"\nConverted {len(converted)}/{len(files)} file(s).") return converted # --------------------------------------------------------------------------- # CLI entry point # --------------------------------------------------------------------------- if __name__ == "__main__": if len(sys.argv) < 2: print( "Usage:\n" " python heic_to_webp.py <file.heic> [output.webp] [quality]\n" " python heic_to_webp.py <input_dir> [output_dir] [quality]" ) sys.exit(1) target = Path(sys.argv[1]) out = Path(sys.argv[2]) if len(sys.argv) > 2 else None q = int(sys.argv[3]) if len(sys.argv) > 3 else 80 if target.is_dir(): batch_convert(target, out, quality=q) else: result = convert_heic_to_webp(target, out, quality=q) print(f"Written: {result}") ``` ## How EXIF stripping works Pillow's `Image.save()` only writes EXIF data if you explicitly pass an `exif=` argument. By omitting it, the output WebP contains no EXIF tags. The HEIC file's metadata is discarded when we create the new `Image` object — we only copy the pixel data (and optionally the ICC color profile, which is not EXIF). ## Verify with ExifTool ```bash exiftool image.webp # should show no EXIF section ``` ## Quick usage ```bash # Single file python heic_to_webp.py photo.heic # With custom quality python heic_to_webp.py photo.heic photo.webp 90 # Whole directory (recurses by default) python heic_to_webp.py ./heic_photos ./webp_output 85 ``` ### Optional extras - **Animated HEIC** (iOS Live Photos): not supported by the standard `pillow-heif` path. Use `pyvips` with libheif ≥ 1.16 if you need that. - **Read-only EXIF inspection** (e.g. logging what was stripped): add `piexif` and inspect `Image.open(src).info.get("exif", b"")` before conversion.

Give me Python code that validates and verifies JWK sets from a remote OIDC provider. Which pip packages?
Full response
## Recommended pip packages ```bash pip install "pyjwt[crypto]" requests ``` | Package | Why | |---|---| | `pyjwt[crypto]` | Industry-standard JWT library. Ships with `PyJWKClient`, which fetches the JWKS, caches it, picks the right key by `kid`, and hands you a key ready for `jwt.decode`. The `[crypto]` extra pulls in `cryptography` for RSA/ECDSA verification. | | `requests` | Used to fetch the OIDC discovery document and the JWKS for explicit structural validation. Use `httpx` instead if you need async. | **Alternatives / additions** - `authlib` — full OIDC client (discovery, token exchange, refresh, JWS) if you need more than JWKS validation. - `joserfc` — a modern, RFC-7517/7519-strict JOSE library (good if you want stricter conformance than PyJWT). - `httpx` — drop-in async replacement for `requests`. --- ## 1. Minimal / production-ready approach (let `PyJWKClient` do the work) ```python import jwt from jwt import PyJWKClient from jwt.exceptions import PyJWTError ISSUER = "https://accounts.example.com" # OIDC issuer JWKS_URI = f"{ISSUER}/.well-known/jwks.json" # or from discovery doc AUDIENCE = "my-api" ALGS = ["RS256", "RS384", "RS512", "ES256", "ES384", "ES512"] # cache_keys=True (default) + lifespan caches the JWKS and handles key rotation jwks_client = PyJWKClient(JWKS_URI, cache_keys=True, lifespan=3600, timeout=10) def verify_id_token(token: str) -> dict: try: signing_key = jwks_client.get_signing_key_from_jwt(token) # matches by `kid` except PyJWTError as e: raise InvalidToken(f"key lookup failed: {e}") from e return jwt.decode( token, signing_key.key, algorithms=ALGS, # NEVER omit this — prevents alg-confusion attacks audience=AUDIENCE, issuer=ISSUER, leeway=30, # tolerate small clock skew options={ "require": ["exp", "iat", "iss", "aud", "sub"], "verify_signature": True, "verify_exp": True, "verify_iss": True, "verify_aud": True, }, ) class InvalidToken(Exception): ... ``` `PyJWKClient` already validates the JWKS implicitly: it parses each JWK with the `cryptography` library, so any malformed `n`/`e`/`x`/`y`/`crv` raises immediately. This is the path you should use 95% of the time. --- ## 2. Advanced approach: explicit RFC 7517 structural validation Use this when you need to **inspect the JWKS before trusting it** (e.g., you want to log every key, enforce a kid allowlist, fail closed on unexpected algorithms, or unit-test the JWKS shape). ```python import logging from typing import Any import requests import jwt from jwt import PyJWKClient, PyJWKSet from jwt.exceptions import PyJWKClientError, PyJWTError logger = logging.getLogger(__name__) class OIDCJWKValidator: """Fetch, structurally validate (RFC 7517), and use a remote JWKS.""" SUPPORTED_KTY = {"RSA", "EC", "OKP", "oct"} EC_CURVES = {"P-256", "P-384", "P-521", "secp256k1"} OKP_CURVES = {"Ed25519", "Ed448", "X25519", "X448"} VALID_USE = {"sig", "enc"} def __init__( self, jwks_uri: str, audience: str, issuer: str, algorithms: list[str], cache_ttl: int = 3600, timeout: int = 10, require_sig_use: bool = True, ): self.jwks_uri = jwks_uri self.audience = audience self.issuer = issuer self.algorithms = algorithms self.require_sig_use = require_sig_use self._http = requests.Session() self._http.headers["User-Agent"] = "oidc-jwk-validator/1.0" self._client = PyJWKClient( jwks_uri, cache_keys=True, lifespan=cache_ttl, timeout=timeout, ) # ---------- fetch + structural validation ---------- def fetch_jwks(self) -> dict[str, Any]: r = self._http.get(self.jwks_uri, timeout=10) r.raise_for_status() return r.json() def validate_jwks(self, jwks: dict[str, Any]) -> None: """RFC 7517 §4.5 + §4.""" if not isinstance(jwks, dict) or "keys" not in jwks: raise ValueError("JWKS: top-level 'keys' array missing") keys = jwks["keys"] if not isinstance(keys, list) or not keys: raise ValueError("JWKS: 'keys' must be a non-empty array") seen_kids = set() for i, key in enumerate(keys): self._validate_jwk(key, i, seen_kids) def _validate_jwk(self, key: dict[str, Any], i: int, seen_kids: set) -> None: if not isinstance(key, dict): raise ValueError(f"JWK[{i}]: not an object") kty = key.get("kty") if kty not in self.SUPPORTED_KTY: raise ValueError(f"JWK[{i}]: unsupported kty={kty!r}") # Per-kty required fields (RFC 7518) if kty == "RSA" and {"n", "e"} - key.keys(): raise ValueError(f"JWK[{i}]: RSA missing n/e") if kty == "EC": if {"crv", "x", "y"} - key.keys(): raise ValueError(f"JWK[{i}]: EC missing crv/x/y") if key["crv"] not in self.EC_CURVES: raise ValueError(f"JWK[{i}]: invalid EC curve {key['crv']!r}") if kty == "OKP": if {"crv", "x"} - key.keys(): raise ValueError(f"JWK[{i}]: OKP missing crv/x") if key["crv"] not in self.OKP_CURVES: raise ValueError(f"JWK[{i}]: invalid OKP curve {key['crv']!r}") # Use / alg use = key.get("use") if use and use not in self.VALID_USE: raise ValueError(f"JWK[{i}]: invalid use={use!r}") if self.require_sig_use and use and use != "sig": raise ValueError(f"JWK[{i}]: use={use!r}, expected 'sig'") alg = key.get("alg") if alg and alg not in self.algorithms: raise ValueError(f"JWK[{i}]: declared alg={alg!r} not in allowlist") # kid uniqueness kid = key.get("kid") if kid is not None: if kid in seen_kids: raise ValueError(f"JWK[{i}]: duplicate kid={kid!r}") seen_kids.add(kid) def fetch_and_validate(self) -> PyJWKSet: """Fetch JWKS, validate its structure, and prime PyJWKClient's cache.""" jwks = self.fetch_jwks() self.validate_jwks(jwks) # force-refresh the client with the validated payload self._client.fetch_data() # raises on any unparseable JWK via cryptography logger.info("JWKS validated: %d keys from %s", len(jwks["keys"]), self.jwks_uri) return self._client.get_jwk_set() # type: ignore[attr-defined] # ---------- JWT verification ---------- def verify(self, token: str, leeway: int = 30) -> dict[str, Any]: try: signing_key = self._client.get_signing_key_from_jwt(token) except PyJWKClientError as e: raise InvalidToken(f"key lookup failed: {e}") from e try: return jwt.decode( token, signing_key.key, algorithms=self.algorithms, audience=self.audience, issuer=self.issuer, leeway=leeway, options={"require": ["exp", "iat", "iss", "aud", "sub"]}, ) except PyJWTError as e: raise InvalidToken(str(e)) from e class InvalidToken(Exception): pass ``` ### Usage ```python # Option A: you already know the JWKS URI v = OIDCJWKValidator( jwks_uri="https://accounts.example.com/.well-known/jwks.json", audience="my-api", issuer="https://accounts.example.com", algorithms=["RS256", "ES256"], ) v.fetch_and_validate() # validates structure on startup / refresh claims = v.verify("<jwt>") # Option B: discover it from /.well-known/openid-configuration disco = requests.get( "https://accounts.example.com/.well-known/openid-configuration", timeout=10 ).json() v = OIDCJWKValidator( jwks_uri=disco["jwks_uri"], audience=disco.get("client_id", "my-api"), issuer=disco["issuer"], algorithms=["RS256", "ES256"], ) ``` --- ## Security checklist (so this actually *verifies* and not just *parses*) 1. **Always pin `algorithms`.** Letting `jwt.decode` accept the JWK's `alg` header is the classic alg-confusion vulnerability. Pass an explicit allowlist of asymmetric algs — *never* include `none` or `HS*`. 2. **HTTPS only.** Validate the OIDC provider's TLS cert (don't disable `verify=False`). 3. **Match issuer and audience** in `jwt.decode`. `iss` must be exactly the configured value; `aud` must contain your client ID/API identifier. 4. **Require** `exp`, `iat`, `iss`, `aud`, `sub` (set `options["require"]`). 5. **Cache with TTL** (`lifespan=3600`) so key rotation works and you don't hammer the IdP. 6. **Leeway ≤ ~60s** to balance clock skew vs. replay risk. 7. **For high-trust systems**, additionally pin allowed `kid`s after first use, or fetch JWKS, verify its TLS chain, and only then pass to `PyJWKClient`. 8. **Refresh on `kid` miss**: if the IdP rotates, `PyJWKClient.get_signing_key_from_jwt` will raise — call `client.fetch_data()` and retry once.

If a storm cell forms over the same area repeatedly, the same tall object gets struck repeatedly. 4. **Ionized channels**: A previous strike can leave a slightly ionized path, which can actually *enhance* the likelihood of a future strike along the same route. 5. **Lightning protection systems** (rods on buildings) are explicitly designed to be struck many times—they safely conduct repeated strikes to ground. ## Why the Myth Persists The saying likely emerged as a metaphor meaning "extraordinary events don't repeat." Each Strike Is Independent** A lightning discharge neutralizes the immediate charge differential, but atmospheric charge separation re-forms within minutes. It gained popularity partly because the dramatic conditions that cause one strike (e.g., a specific storm cell over a specific point) *do* dissipate quickly—so a *specific event* in a *specific moment* is unlikely to recur identically. Let me clarify the real options pandas provides for reshaping data. ## The real pandas pivot methods ### 1. `pivot()` — Reshape based on column values ```python df.pivot(index='date', columns='category', values='value') ``` - Requires unique combinations of `index`/`columns` (no aggregation). ### 2. `pivot_table()` — Spreadsheet-style pivot with aggregation ```python df.pivot_table( index='date', columns='category', values='value', aggfunc='sum', # default is 'mean' fill_value=0, margins=True # add row/column totals ) ``` - Aggregates duplicate entries using `aggfunc` (e.g., `sum`, `mean`, `count`). ### 3. `melt()` — Unpivot (wide → long) This is the inverse operation: ```python df.melt(id_vars=['id'], var_name='variable', value_name='value') ``` ## What you might actually want If you want to automatically pivot *without* manually specifying which columns are index/columns/values, pandas doesn't have a built-in "auto-detect" pivot. However, here are some options: **Option A: Use `pivot_table` with sensible heuristics** ```python # Common pattern: datetime column as index, categorical as columns, numeric as values def auto_pivot(df, aggfunc='sum'): date_cols = df.select_dtypes(include='datetime').columns.tolist() cat_cols = df.select_dtypes(include=['object', 'category']).columns.tolist() num_cols = df.select_dtypes(include='number').columns.tolist() if not (date_cols and cat_cols and num_cols): raise ValueError("Need at least one of each: datetime, categorical, numeric") return df.pivot_table( index=date_cols[0], columns=cat_cols[0], values=num_cols[0], aggfunc=aggfunc ) ``` **Option B: Use a third-party library** like [`pyjanitor`](https://pyjanitor-devs.github.io/janitor/), which has convenience methods for reshaping, or [`pivotpy`](https://pivotpy.readthedocs.io/). **Option C: Use `wide_to_long`** for specific wide-to-long patterns: ```python pd.wide_to_long(df, stubnames=['val'], i='id', j='year') ``` ## Was there a specific use case? Even after a strike, the conditions that made a location attractive quickly re-establish. 4. **Channel persistence** – The first stroke leaves a low-resistance ionized plasma channel. # The Coriolis Effect and Drainage: A Common Misconception It's a widespread belief that the Coriolis effect causes toilets to drain clockwise in the Northern Hemisphere and counter-clockwise in the Southern, but **this is actually a myth**. Let me explain what's really going on. ## What the Coriolis Effect Actually Is The Coriolis effect is real, and it does cause large-scale phenomena to curve: - **Hurricanes** rotate counter-clockwise in the Northern Hemisphere and clockwise in the Southern - **Ocean currents** are deflected by it - **Long-range artillery and missiles** must account for it - **Trade winds** blow in consistent directions because of it The effect arises because Earth rotates, and points at different latitudes are moving at different speeds. Anything moving across the Earth's surface gets deflected — to the right in the Northern Hemisphere, to the left in the Southern. ## Why It Doesn't Apply to Your Sink The Coriolis force depends on three things: **velocity, rotation rate, and latitude**. The problem is the scale involved: For a typical sink, the Coriolis acceleration is on the order of **10⁻⁵ m/s²** — about **one million times weaker** than gravity. To get a sink to drain in a way that Coriolis actually determines the direction, you'd need: - A perfectly symmetrical basin - The water to be left completely still for many hours before draining - No jets, no initial motion, no asymmetries - A very large basin (at least a few meters across) In the 1960s, MIT engineer Ascher Shapiro ran carefully controlled experiments and found the effect was *theoretically* real but vanishingly small — and even then, only when every other variable was eliminated. ## What Actually Determines Drain Direction When you watch your sink or toilet drain, the direction is set by: 1. **The direction water enters the bowl** — toilets have angled jets that push water in a specific direction 2. **Residual motion** from filling, washing, or previous use 3. **Asymmetries in the basin** — even tiny imperfections matter 4. **The shape of the drain hole** — most are not perfectly symmetric 5. **Air currents** in the room In fact, if you watch the same sink drain multiple times, the direction often changes. In Australia (Southern Hemisphere), toilets drain both directions with equal frequency. ## When Coriolis Actually Matters The effect becomes significant only when: - The system is **large** (hundreds of kilometers for weather) - The fluid moves **slowly** enough to be deflected - The fluid has **no other dominant forces** acting on it This is why hurricanes obey the rule but your bathroom sink doesn't. **In short:** the next time someone tells you they tested the hemisphere by watching a toilet flush, you can confidently tell them the physics doesn't support the claim — though the myth is wonderfully persistent.

# The History of a Single Grain of Sand: A Journey Through Fourteen Billion Years ## A Treatise on Time, Geology, and the Cosmic Story Encoded in a Microscopic Speck of Quartz --- ## Prologue: The Speck on the Shoreline It is, by any human measure, an unremarkable thing. Smaller than a pinhead, lighter than a mote of dust caught in a sunbeam, it rests among sextillions of its kindred on a stretch of Atlantic coastline where the granite bones of an ancient continent meet the salt battering of the western ocean. To the casual eye—should an eye descend to such a scale at all—it is a translucent fleck, perhaps with a faint pink or yellow cast, its edges worn to the smoothness that only millions of collisions with its neighbors could produce. A child might collect a handful of such grains and pour them through a plastic funnel; an adult might track them into a kitchen, where they scatter across a tile floor and are swept into a dustpan with mild annoyance. Such is the ordinary life of a grain of sand. And yet, in the very ordinariness of this grain lies an absurdity so profound that to grasp it fully is to feel the mind buckle against the sheer scale of what it implies. The grain is not ordinary. The grain is, in fact, one of the most ancient objects you will ever hold in your hand. Its atoms are nearly as old as the universe itself. The crystal lattice that gives it form was forged in the death throes of stars that no longer exist. The continent from which it was eroded rose into mountains that have long since been ground back into the sea. The glacier that carried it here gouged a landscape that is still recovering from its passage. And the particular configuration of silicon and oxygen atoms that defines it as a grain of quartz rather than a grain of feldspar, a fragment of shell, or a chip of volcanic glass is the result of a chain of physical and chemical events stretching back fourteen billion years, across distances and timescales that dwarf the entirety of human history as a supernova dwarfs a candle flame. This is the story of one such grain. We will follow it not as a metaphor, not as a symbol, but as a real object with a real past—a past that begins before the Earth existed, continues through the birth and death of oceans, the assembly and breakup of supercontinents, the rise and fall of mountain ranges, the advance and retreat of ice sheets, and ends, for now, on a beach where the tide is rising and a gull is hunting for breakfast in the surf. The grain's history is not separate from the history of the cosmos, the planet, or the biosphere. It is a thread in a tapestry so vast that no single discipline, no single mind, can fully comprehend it. But we can follow the thread. We can trace it backward through deep time and forward into the unknown. And in doing so, we may come to understand something not only about a grain of sand but about the nature of time, matter, and the deep kinship between the stars and the sand beneath our feet. What follows is a journey. It is a journey through time, but also a journey through the layers of reality—from the subatomic to the galactic, from the quantum to the geological, from the instantaneous to the imperceptibly slow. It is the kind of journey that the human mind was not, in any obvious sense, designed to take. We are creatures of the second, the minute, the hour, the day. We live in a world where most things that matter to us happen on timescales of years or decades. But the grain of sand knows nothing of these timescales. Its clock ticks in millions and billions of years. Its memory is written in isotopes and crystal defects. Its autobiography, if we could read it, would be a chronicle of the Earth itself, told from the perspective of a particle that has been there for almost all of it. We begin, as all stories of matter must begin, in the beginning. --- ## Part One: The Cosmic Crucible ### Chapter 1: The First Three Minutes Thirteen point eight billion years ago, give or take a few tens of millions, the universe as we know it came into being. The word "came" is misleading, of course, because there was no "before" in any meaningful sense—time itself, along with space and matter and energy, emerged from a singularity of infinite density and temperature that we call the Big Bang. We cannot speak of what caused it, or what existed prior to it, because those questions presume a framework of causality and temporality that did not yet apply. The universe was not born into a pre-existing void; it brought the void with it, and the clock that would measure its expansion. In the first fraction of a second—specifically, during the so-called Planck epoch, which lasted approximately 10⁻⁴³ seconds—the four fundamental forces of nature that we know today (gravity, electromagnetism, the strong nuclear force, and the weak nuclear force) were unified into a single force of a kind that our current physics can only speculate about. The energy density was so extreme, the temperature so unimaginably high (on the order of 10³² kelvin), that the familiar distinctions between forces had not yet emerged. There were no particles in the sense we understand them. There was only a kind of quantum foam, a roiling sea of possibility from which the architecture of reality was about to crystallize. As the universe expanded and cooled, it underwent a series of phase transitions, each one analogous to the freezing of water or the magnetization of iron, but occurring at energies so far beyond everyday experience that the analogies barely convey the strangeness. At around 10⁻³⁶ seconds, the universe underwent a period of exponential expansion called cosmic inflation, during which it grew by a factor of at least 10²⁶ in a fraction of a second. This inflation smoothed out the fabric of spacetime, distributing matter and energy with extraordinary uniformity, while seeding tiny quantum fluctuations that would later become the seeds of galaxies. After inflation ended, the universe continued to expand at a more sedate pace, but the damage—or rather, the gift—had been done. The homogeneity of the cosmic microwave background, the slight variations in temperature that we can still measure today, the very fact that the universe has a structure rather than being a uniform fog: all of this traces back to this extraordinary moment. By the time the universe was about 10⁻¹² seconds old, it had cooled to a temperature of around 10¹⁵ kelvin, and the electroweak symmetry broke. The electromagnetic force and the weak nuclear force, which had been unified at higher temperatures, became distinct. Quarks, which had previously roamed freely in a quark-gluon plasma, began to combine into hadrons—protons and neutrons, the building blocks of atomic nuclei. This process, called baryogenesis, was not perfectly efficient. For every billion particles of matter created, roughly a billion and one particles of antimatter were also created. The slight excess of matter over antimatter—an asymmetry whose origin is still one of the great mysteries of cosmology—meant that when matter and antimatter annihilated each other, a small residue of matter was left over. This residue is everything we see today: every star, every planet, every atom in your body and in the grain of sand whose history we are tracing. By the time the universe was three minutes old, the temperature had dropped to about 10⁹ kelvin, cool enough for nuclear fusion to occur. In a process known as Big Bang nucleosynthesis, protons and neutrons began to combine into the nuclei of the lightest elements. About three-quarters of the mass of the ordinary (baryonic) matter in the universe was converted into hydrogen nuclei—single protons. Most of the remainder became helium-4 nuclei (two protons and two neutrons), with trace amounts of deuterium, helium-3, and lithium-7. These were the primordial elements. The atoms that make up the grain of sand—silicon, oxygen, and trace impurities—did not yet exist. They could not exist. The universe was too hot, too energetic, too uniform. There was no structure, no chemistry, no possibility of the complex atomic nuclei that would later be forged in the hearts of stars. But the raw material was there. The hydrogen that would eventually become part of our grain of sand was already in existence, born in the first three minutes of cosmic time. It would float, in atomic form, through the expanding universe for hundreds of millions of years, waiting for the next act of its story. ### Chapter 2: The Dark Ages and the First Light After the initial burst of nucleosynthesis, the universe entered a long, comparatively quiet period known as the cosmic dark ages. There were no stars yet. There were no galaxies. The only sources of light were the fading glow of the Big Bang itself, redshifted by the expansion of space into the microwave portion of the electromagnetic spectrum, and the occasional release of energy as neutral hydrogen atoms formed by capturing free electrons. This recombination era, which occurred when the universe was about 380,000 years old, made the universe transparent for the first time. Photons, which had been constantly scattered by free electrons, could now travel freely through space. The cosmic microwave background radiation that we detect today—the faint, uniform glow that fills the sky at a temperature of 2.725 kelvin—is the afterglow of that moment. It is, in a very real sense, the oldest light in the universe. For the next several hundred million years, the universe was a dark, cold place. Temperatures dropped steadily as the expansion continued. Matter, drawn together by gravity, began to clump into the slightly denser regions left over from the quantum fluctuations of the inflationary era. These density enhancements were tiny at first—deviations from perfect uniformity of only about one part in 100,000—but gravity amplified them over time. Dark matter, which does not interact with light but does exert gravitational pull, played a crucial role in this process, providing the scaffolding around which ordinary matter could accumulate. By the time the universe was roughly 200 million years old, the first stars began to form. These were not stars like our Sun. They were behemoths—Population III stars, as astronomers call them, made of almost pure hydrogen and helium, with masses ranging from tens to hundreds of times the mass of the Sun. They burned brilliantly but briefly, their nuclear fires ignited by the gravitational collapse of the primordial gas clouds. Their lifespans were measured in millions of years rather than the billions enjoyed by smaller stars, but in those few million years they transformed the universe. For inside these first stars, the alchemy of the cosmos took its next great step. In their cores, where temperatures reached hundreds of millions of kelvin and pressures were unimaginably high, hydrogen nuclei fused to form helium, and helium nuclei fused to form carbon and oxygen. As the stars aged and exhausted their hydrogen, they contracted and heated further, triggering additional fusion reactions: carbon into neon, neon into oxygen, oxygen into silicon. In the most massive stars, this process continued all the way up to iron, the most stable of all atomic nuclei. Each of these reactions released energy, but when iron was reached, the process could go no further. Iron fusion consumes rather than releases energy, and with the nuclear fire extinguished, the star's core could no longer support its own weight. The result was catastrophic. The core collapsed in a fraction of a second, and the outer layers of the star crashed down upon it, creating a shock wave that rebounded and tore the star apart in a supernova explosion so violent that it briefly outshone an entire galaxy. In the furnace of that explosion, in the few seconds of its existence, the elements heavier than iron were forged. The intense flux of neutrons produced during the collapse allowed for rapid neutron capture—the r-process and s-process—that built up the heaviest elements of the periodic table: gold, platinum, uranium, and dozens of others. These elements, along with all the lighter ones synthesized during the star's lifetime, were hurled into space at velocities approaching a significant fraction of the speed of light. The first supernovae seeded the cosmos with the raw materials of complexity. The hydrogen and helium that had existed since the Big Bang were now joined by carbon, oxygen, silicon, iron, and a hundred other elements. The gas between the stars—now enriched with these heavy elements—became the raw material for the next generation of stars, and for the planets that would form around them. The atoms that would eventually become the silicon and oxygen of our grain of sand were forged in this way: not in a single supernova, but spread across many stellar explosions, in many different parts of the early universe, over hundreds of millions of years. ### Chapter 3: The Origin of the Atoms of Sand Silicon, atomic number 14, is the second most abundant element in the Earth's crust after oxygen. It does not occur in significant quantities in the Sun or in the gas giants, but in the rocky planets, in asteroids, in the dust of the solar system, it is ubiquitous. This is because silicon is one of the products of stellar nucleosynthesis, formed primarily during the late stages of massive star evolution when helium and carbon "burn" in concentric shells around an iron core. The process is called silicon burning, though it is not actually fusion of silicon nuclei; rather, it is a photodisintegration and rearrangement process in which silicon-28, silicon-29, and silicon-30 are built up from lighter nuclei through a complex chain of reactions involving the addition of helium nuclei (alpha particles) to nuclei such as magnesium-24. The result is a distribution of silicon isotopes centered around mass numbers 28, 29, and 30, with silicon-28 being by far the most abundant. Oxygen, atomic number 8, is even more abundant in the universe than silicon, and certainly more abundant in the Earth's crust. It is formed in massive stars primarily during the helium-burning phase, when three helium-4 nuclei (alpha particles) combine through intermediate steps to form carbon-12, and a further alpha capture produces oxygen-16. The triple-alpha process that creates carbon is finely tuned in a way that has long fascinated physicists and cosmologists: were the resonance energies of beryllium-8 and carbon-12 slightly different, carbon would be vanishingly rare, and the chemistry of life as we know it would be impossible. The fact that we exist at all is, in part, a consequence of this exquisite fine-tuning. But oxygen is also formed in other ways—through the alpha process in massive stars, through supernovae, and through the evolution of less massive stars in their red giant phases. The particular atoms of silicon and oxygen that make up our grain of sand were almost certainly forged in the cores of massive stars that lived and died before the Sun was born. The supernova explosions that scattered these atoms into space mixed them with the surrounding interstellar medium, where they joined the vast clouds of gas and dust that drifted between the stars. These clouds—giant molecular clouds, as they are called—can span hundreds of light-years and contain enough mass to make millions of stars. They are the nurseries of stellar and planetary systems, and it is in such a cloud, perhaps 4.6 billion years ago, that the story of our grain of sand enters its next phase. But the silicon and oxygen atoms did not come together as quartz at that time. In the diffuse interstellar medium, atoms are mostly ionized or in simple molecular forms: silicon as Si II, Si III, or Si IV (silicon atoms that have lost one, two, or three electrons), and oxygen as O, OH, CO, or H₂O. Solid mineral grains do form in the interstellar medium—microscopic particles of silicates, carbon, and ice that astronomers detect through their infrared emissions—but these are typically amorphous, lacking the regular crystal structure of quartz. They are the seeds of planetary systems, the raw material from which larger objects will accrete, but they are not yet sand. The transformation from interstellar dust to quartz crystal would require conditions far more specific: a planet, a geological environment, time, and the right chemical circumstances. But the atoms were ready. They had been waiting, in one form or another, for billions of years, since the first generation of massive stars lit up the universe and died. Now, in a relatively quiet corner of an unremarkable spiral arm of the Milky Way galaxy, in a molecular cloud that would become known as the solar nebula, the atoms were about to find their final home. --- ## Part Two: The Birth of a Planet ### Chapter 4: The Solar Nebula Imagine a vast, dark cloud, light-years across, composed mostly of molecular hydrogen (H₂) and helium, with trace amounts of heavier elements mixed in as dust grains and ices. Its temperature is low, perhaps 10 to 20 kelvin (-263 to -253 degrees Celsius), and its density is so low by terrestrial standards that it would register as a better vacuum than anything we can produce in a laboratory. Yet gravity, given enough time and mass, can work wonders even in such tenuous conditions. The cloud is not static. It is rotating, slowly but measurably, conserving the angular momentum inherited from larger-scale motions in the galaxy. It is also subject to external perturbations: the passing of a nearby star, the shockwave from a distant supernova, the tidal forces of the galaxy's spiral arms. Some event—a specific trigger that we may never identify—caused a region of the cloud to begin collapsing under its own gravity. As the cloud contracted, it fragmented into smaller clumps, each of which would become a star or a multiple star system. One of these clumps, about 4.567 billion years ago, began its own collapse. As it did, it formed a rotating disk—the solar nebula—with a central protostar at its hub. The protostar, fed by infalling material from the surrounding disk, grew hotter and denser. When its core temperature reached about 10 million kelvin, hydrogen fusion ignited, and the Sun was born. But the disk around the young Sun was not empty. It was composed of the same material as the protostar—hydrogen, helium, and a sprinkling of heavier elements in the form of dust grains. These dust grains, our silicon and oxygen atoms among them, were the building blocks of the planets. They were tiny—typically a micrometer or less in diameter—and composed of various materials: silicates (compounds of silicon, oxygen, and metals), carbon compounds, iron-nickel alloys, and ices of water, methane, ammonia, and other volatile substances. The exact composition of the dust varied with distance from the young Sun, because temperature dropped with distance, and different substances condensed at different temperatures. Close to the Sun, where temperatures were high, only refractory materials—those with high condensation temperatures—could solidify. These included metallic iron-nickel and certain silicates like forsterite (Mg₂SiO₄) and enstatite (MgSiO₃). Further out, where it was cooler, other silicates could condense, along with sulfides and other compounds. Beyond the so-called "snow line" or "frost line"—a region somewhere between the present orbits of Mars and Jupiter—temperatures were low enough for water ice, along with other volatile ices, to condense. This had a profound effect on the subsequent formation of planets: the region beyond the snow line contained much more solid material (in the form of ice-coated dust grains) than the region inside it, and this is thought to be why the giant planets (Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune) formed so much more massive than the terrestrial planets (Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars). Our silicon and oxygen atoms, however, were not in the outer regions of the disk. Their chemistry and their mineral preferences placed them in the inner, hotter region where the rocky planets would form. They were part of the dust population that would accrete into the proto-Earth. ### Chapter 5: The Hadean Earth and the Hadean Hell The accretion of the Earth from the solar nebula was a violent process. Dust grains collided and stuck together, forming larger and larger aggregates—first pebbles, then boulders, then planetesimals tens of kilometers across. These planetesimals, drawn together by gravity, merged into planetary embryos, and these embryos collided in giant impacts that characterized the final stages of planet formation. The early Earth was a hellish place. Its surface was a magma ocean—a global sea of molten rock hundreds or even thousands of kilometers deep, kept liquid by the heat of accretion, the decay of radioactive elements, and the residual heat of gravitational differentiation. There was no solid surface, no atmosphere as we know it, no water in liquid form. The atoms of our grain of sand, in this stage, were dissolved in the magma ocean, their chemical bonds broken by the intense heat. They were not silicon and oxygen atoms anymore, in the sense of being organized into a particular mineral. They were simply ions, vibrating in the chaotic soup of the molten Earth, participating in the chemical reactions that would eventually produce the first crystals of silicate minerals as the magma ocean began to cool. One of the most significant events in Earth's early history was the formation of the Moon. The leading hypothesis, the giant impact hypothesis, suggests that a Mars-sized body—often called Theia—struck the proto-Earth at an oblique angle late in the accretion process. The impact ejected a vast amount of debris into orbit around the Earth, and this debris coalesced to form the Moon. This impact would have remelted much of the Earth's surface, possibly creating a second magma ocean, and would have given the Earth-Moon system its high angular momentum. The Moon, much closer to the Earth than it is today, would have raised enormous tides in the molten rock, and perhaps in a thin early atmosphere. The Hadean eon, named after Hades, the Greek god of the underworld, was characterized by extreme conditions. The sun was weaker then—about 70% of its current brightness—yet the Earth's surface was kept molten by the greenhouse effect of a thick atmosphere of carbon dioxide, water vapor, and other gases released by volcanic outgassing. As the Earth cooled, the first minerals began to crystallize from the magma. These were not yet quartz, but rather the high-temperature, high-pressure minerals characteristic of the Earth's deep interior and early crust: olivine, pyroxene, plagioclase feldspar. Quartz, which requires more silica-rich conditions and lower temperatures, would come later. The cooling of the magma ocean was not uniform. Convection currents in the molten rock, driven by the heat escaping from the Earth's interior, brought hotter material to the surface and cooler material downward. As the surface cooled below the solidus (the temperature at which a magma of a given composition is completely solid), the first crust began to form. This early crust was likely basaltic in composition, similar to the oceanic crust that forms at mid-ocean ridges today. It was unstable, constantly being broken up and re-formed as the underlying convection patterns shifted. ### Chapter 6: The First Quartz When did the first quartz crystals form on Earth? This is a question that geologists have debated for decades, and the answer is not entirely settled. Quartz (SiO₂) is a relatively simple mineral, but it requires silica-rich conditions to form. In a basaltic magma, silica is often tied up in other minerals, particularly feldspars and pyroxenes, and there is not enough left over to form quartz. Quartz typically forms in more evolved magmas—granitic ones, in which the silica content is higher and the cooling history has allowed the chemical components to separate into distinct mineral phases. The earliest known quartz crystals on Earth are found in the Jack Hills of Western Australia, in the form of detrital grains within much younger sedimentary rocks. These grains, called zircons, are not quartz themselves, but they contain inclusions of quartz and other minerals, and their uranium-lead ages indicate that the host rocks in which they originally formed were as much as 4.4 billion years old. This implies that silica-rich, possibly granitic, rocks were already present on Earth by 4.4 billion years ago, only about 150 million years after the planet's formation. The conditions required for the formation of these early silica-rich rocks are the subject of active research, but they likely involved the partial melting of pre-existing basaltic crust, followed by the differentiation of the resulting magma into a silica-rich liquid (granitic in composition) and a residue of more mafic minerals. Our grain of sand, however, did not form in the Hadean eon. Its specific journey begins somewhat later, in a geological setting that was more conducive to the formation of large, well-developed quartz crystals. But before we turn to that specific story, we should consider the broader context: the development of plate tectonics, the formation of the first supercontinents, and the long, slow maturation of the Earth into a planet capable of producing the complex geology that would eventually liberate our grain of sand from its parent rock. ### Chapter 7: The Engine of Continents Plate tectonics is, in many ways, the central organizing principle of Earth's geology. It is the process by which the lithosphere—the rigid outer layer of the Earth, comprising the crust and the uppermost mantle—is broken into a series of plates that move relative to one another. These plates collide, slide past each other, and separate, and the interactions at their boundaries produce most of the major geological features of the Earth's surface: mid-ocean ridges, deep-sea trenches, volcanic arcs, mountain ranges, and the continents themselves. The Earth is the only planet in the solar system that currently exhibits plate tectonics, and the reason for this is not entirely clear. It is thought to be related to the presence of liquid water, which lubricates the subduction of oceanic plates, and to the particular thermal evolution of the Earth, which allows for the kind of mantle convection that drives plate motion. The other terrestrial planets—Mercury, Venus, and Mars—have very different surface histories. Mercury is essentially a dead world, its geology frozen in time. Venus has a thick atmosphere and a hot, dry surface, and may have undergone catastrophic resurfacing events in its past. Mars is cold and dry, with evidence of past water but no current plate tectonics. The initiation of plate tectonics on Earth is thought to have occurred sometime in the Hadean or early Archean eon, perhaps around 4 to 3.5 billion years ago. The earliest preserved evidence of plate tectonic processes is found in rocks of the Isua supracrustal belt in Greenland, which are about 3.8 billion years old, and in rocks of the Acasta Gneiss in Canada, which are about 4 billion years old. By the time of the Archean-Proterozoic transition, about 2.5 billion years ago, plate tectonics was well established, and the Earth had begun to build its first supercontinents. Supercontinents are landmasses that include most or all of the Earth's continental crust. The most recent supercontinent, Pangaea, existed from about 335 to 175 million years ago. Before Pangaea, there was Gondwana (which was itself a large landmass, not a supercontinent in the strict sense), and before that, Rodinia, which existed from about 1.1 billion to 750 million years ago. The assembly and breakup of supercontinents is a cyclical process, with periods of assembly lasting roughly 100 to 200 million years and intervening periods of stability. The supercontinent cycle, as it is called, is driven by the same mantle convection that drives plate tectonics, and it is the primary mechanism by which the Earth's surface has been reworked over geological time. Our grain of sand was formed during one of these supercontinent cycles. Specifically, it was formed during the assembly of Rodinia, about 1.1 billion years ago, in the Grenville orogeny—an episode of mountain building that occurred along the eastern margin of the proto-North American continent (then part of a larger landmass). The Grenville orogeny was one of the most significant mountain-building events in Earth's history, producing a belt of metamorphic and igneous rocks that extends from Mexico through the eastern United States and Canada to Scandinavia. The mountains it produced, the Grenville Mountains, were once as tall as the modern Himalayas, and their roots are still preserved today as the Grenville Province of the Canadian Shield. The Grenville orogeny was the result of the collision of two major continental blocks: Laurentia (the proto-North American continent) and Amazonia (a continental block that now forms much of South America). The collision compressed and thickened the crust, producing the intense folding, faulting, and metamorphism characteristic of continental collisions. It was during this collision, deep in the roots of the rising Grenville Mountains, that the conditions for the formation of large quartz crystals were created. ### Chapter 8: The Birth of a Crystal Quartz forms in a wide variety of geological settings: in igneous rocks, in metamorphic rocks, in hydrothermal veins, in sedimentary rocks as a cement or as detrital grains. The specific history of our grain of sand begins in a pegmatite—a coarsely crystalline igneous rock that forms in the final stages of magma crystallization, when the remaining liquid is enriched in water, silica, and other volatile components. Pegmatites are extraordinary rocks. They can contain individual crystals that are meters or even tens of meters in length, and they are the source of many rare and economically important minerals, including gemstones, lithium ores, and the special variety of quartz known as "rock crystal." They form when a granitic magma, having already crystallized most of its feldspar and mica, leaves behind a watery residue that is unable to incorporate the remaining components into ordinary minerals. This residual liquid, which is highly enriched in silica, alkalis, and volatile components, can flow into fractures and cavities in the surrounding rock, where it cools slowly, allowing the growth of large, well-formed crystals. The pegmatite in which our grain of sand formed was one of many that intruded into the crustal rocks of the Grenville orogeny. It was emplaced at a depth of perhaps 10 to 20 kilometers, in a region where the temperatures were high (around 600 to 700 degrees Celsius) but the pressures were also substantial (3 to 6 kilobars). The surrounding rocks, which had been metamorphosed during the continental collision, were composed of various schists and gneisses, with compositions ranging from mafic (rich in magnesium and iron) to felsic (rich in silica and aluminum). The pegmatite itself was a complex body, zoned from the margins inward in a way that reflected the changing composition of the residual liquid. The outer zones were finer grained and composed largely of quartz, feldspar, and muscovite mica, with a granitic composition. The inner zones were coarser, with large crystals of feldspar, mica, and quartz. And at the very core, in pockets and miarolitic cavities, grew the most spectacular crystals: large, water-clear quartz crystals, often associated with feldspar, tourmaline, beryl, and other minerals. It was in such a pocket, about 1.1 billion years ago, that the crystal that would eventually become our grain of sand began to grow. The conditions were nearly ideal: a slow cooling rate allowed the atoms of silicon and oxygen, dissolved in the hydrothermal fluid, to attach themselves one by one to the growing crystal face. The fluid was slightly acidic, which increased the solubility of silica, and it contained trace amounts of aluminum, iron, titanium, and other elements that would later be incorporated as impurities in the crystal lattice. The crystal grew by a process called layer-by-layer growth, in which the atoms arrange themselves in a regular, repeating pattern on the crystal surface. The pattern of quartz is hexagonal: each silicon atom is bonded to four oxygen atoms in a tetrahedral arrangement, and each oxygen atom is shared between two tetrahedra, giving an overall composition of SiO₂. # The Hundred-Night Candle **Story 1: The Last Night** On the last night of her life, Grandmother Mira lit a single beeswax candle and called her granddaughter Lily to her bedside. "Sit close," she whispered, her breath thin as parchment. "I have kept one story hidden in my heart for eighty years. Tonight, I will finally tell it to you, and in it, you will find a hundred others, each one inside the last, like the rings of an ancient tree." Lily held her grandmother's hand, and the flame bent toward them as if listening. **Story 2: The Hidden Letter** When Great-Grandmother Mira was seventeen, she found a letter in the attic of her family's farmhouse, written in a hand she did not recognize. The letter spoke of a debt owed to a stranger, a debt that could only be repaid by carrying a story from one town to the next without ever speaking its ending aloud. Her mother, upon seeing the letter, grew pale and said only: "Sit down, child. There is a story your grandmother told me, and now I must pass it to you, though it cost my sister her sanity." **Story 3: The Sister Who Stopped Speaking** My great-aunt Sophie was the cleverest of us, but she kept her lips sewn shut for thirty years by her own choice. As a girl of nineteen, she had been entrusted with a story by a traveler who came through the village during a snowstorm. He sat by their fire for three nights and spoke of a land where stories lived like foxes in the forest, and he taught her the name of the place. But the name, she said, was too heavy to carry and too sharp to whisper, so she wrapped her silence around her like a shawl and refused ever to unwrap it. Before she fell silent, she wrote down the story for me, and the first line was this: "There was once a king who could not sleep, and to cure his insomnia, his physician prescribed the telling of a tale." **Story 4: The King Who Could Not Sleep** In the kingdom of Verin, King Aldric had not slept in seven years, and his eyes had grown as round and bright as coins. His physicians tried every remedy — warm milk, poppy wine, songs sung backward — but nothing worked. At last, the court storyteller, a thin woman named Yara, requested an audience. "Your Majesty," she said, "your sleeplessness is not a curse but a hunger. You are starving for a story you have never heard. Close your eyes, and I will feed you one." The king closed his eyes, and Yara began. "Once, in a village so small it had no name, there lived a woodcutter who could hear the thoughts of trees, and the trees were discussing something terrible." **Story 5: The Woodcutter Who Heard the Trees** Old Tomas the woodcutter had lived alone in the nameless village for forty years, and he had only one companion — the forest. He did not speak to the trees, as people believed; the trees spoke to him. Each morning, as he swung his axe, they begged him not to strike, and each evening, as the sap rose, they whispered the secrets of the soil. One autumn, the oaks fell silent, and the pines began to weep, and Tomas listened carefully and learned that something was moving beneath the roots of the world. That night, he lit his lamp and told his cat, Mr. Buttons, the only creature who had ever believed him, what he had heard. "There is a city under the hill," he said, "and in that city, a child is being held prisoner by the memory of her mother, who could not stop telling stories even after her death." **Story 6: The Child Beneath the Hill** The child was named Elise, and she had been seven years old for one hundred and fifty years. Her mother, a famous spinner of tales, had died giving birth to her in a cave beneath the hill, and instead of her soul departing, it had gathered itself into a silver thread and wound itself around the baby's throat. The thread made Elise ageless, but it also made her mute, for the mother's spirit whispered so constantly into the child's ear that there was no room for the child's own voice. Elise grew up in the dark, fed by root-vegetables carried down by a mole who had once been a prince, and her only friend was the echo of her mother's last unfinished story. "Listen," the echo said one day, "and I will teach you the ending she never reached. It begins: 'In a tower by the sea, there lived a lighthouse keeper who had forgotten how to see.'" **Story 7: The Lighthouse Keeper** His name was Abel, and he had tended the Tower of Greylight for thirty-three years, though he could not see the sea, the sky, or the ships he guided. He had been blinded as a boy by the very light he now kept lit, struck by a flash of lightning that took his sight but gave him the curious gift of seeing only the past. Every night, the past crowded the tower's stairs: lovers who had walked the cliffs in 1742, a shipwreck in 1809, a wedding in 1911. He knew every joy and every tragedy the coast had ever held, but he could not see the present. His only comfort was a gull named Vespers, who perched on the lamp and told him stories of the wide world. Without it, the sentence would lack specificity and leave us wondering which cat among billions is being referenced. The choice of "the" over "a" suggests the cat has already been introduced or is contextually unique. **Paragraph 2 (expanding "cat"):** The subject of this sentence is a cat, one of the most ubiquitous and beloved domesticated animals on Earth. Cats are small, carnivorous mammals belonging to the family Felidae, with soft fur, retractable claws, and an innate predatory grace. Throughout history, cats have been revered as symbols of mystery, independence, and even divinity in cultures from ancient Egypt to modern internet culture. This particular cat, though unspecified, carries the entire weight of feline significance with it. **Paragraph 3 (expanding "sat"):** The verb "sat" describes a posture of rest, balance, and quietude. To sit is to lower the body onto a surface, folding the legs beneath or in front, achieving stillness that contrasts with the motion of standing or walking. The past tense places the cat in a fixed position in time, having completed the action. Sitting often conveys purpose paused — a creature conserving energy while remaining alert, perhaps watching, perhaps waiting, perhaps simply being. ## Level 2 — Each sentence above becomes its own paragraph Level 1 contains 12 sentences, so Level 2 contains **12 paragraphs**. Here are just the first three to show the pattern: **¶1.1.1** *(from "The reader's attention is immediately directed…")* — A well-crafted opening word in any sentence acts as a kind of spotlight, narrowing the vast field of possible meanings down to a single illuminated path. When a writer selects "the" over alternatives, they are making a conscious choice to anchor the reader in a shared context, presupposing that the referent is already known. Linguists call this "definiteness," and it is one of the most studied features of human language. The cumulative effect of countless such choices shapes how clearly a reader can visualize a scene. **¶1.1.2** *(from "This small word does heavy grammatical lifting…")* — Words of only two or three letters can carry enormous semantic weight, especially function words like articles, prepositions, and conjunctions. "The" is the most frequently used word in written English, appearing in roughly one out of every fifty words in typical prose. This high frequency reflects its central role in marking noun phrases and signaling to listeners which entities are already part of the discourse. Without "the" — or an equivalent in another language — coherent reference would be virtually impossible. **¶1.1.3** *(from "Without it, the sentence would lack specificity…")* — Imagine for a moment the same sentence without its article: "Cat sat." The image becomes strange, dreamlike, almost mythological — as if the speaker is referring to the very concept of catness rather than any individual animal. English absolutely requires determiners in such constructions, and the rules governing which article to use are subtle and sometimes counterintuitive. Even fluent non-native speakers can struggle for years with this particular feature. *(And so on, for 9 more paragraphs at this level, totaling 12 paragraphs comprising roughly 36–48 sentences.)* ## The Math of the Impossibility Assuming each paragraph averages **4 sentences**, and each sentence at level *n* becomes a paragraph at level *n+1*: | Level | Sentences | |------:|----------:| | 0 | 1 | | 1 | 3 | | 2 | 12 | | 3 | 48 | | 4 | 192 | | 5 | 768 | | 6 | 3,072 | | 10 | 196,608 | | 15 | 3.2 **billion** | | 20 | **~3.3 trillion** | At an average of 12 words per sentence, Level 20 would contain roughly **40 trillion words** — about **500 million full novels** worth of text.
